title: Timeline
full_review:
����������A team of student archeologists must travel back in time to rescue their professor trapped in the 14th century in the stale sci-fi actioner "Timeline" (Paramount).

Despite an intriguing premise, the film, helmed by veteran director Richard Donner ("Lethal Weapon" and "Superman"), is weighed down by an embarrassing script and acting that couldn't be stiffer if they performed in suits of rusted armor. Compared to sitting through this clunker, life in the 1300s with its occasional black plague or turn on the rack seems downright appealing.

Based on author Michael Crichton's novel, "Timeline" tells the story of a group of preternaturally good-looking archeologists-in-training (including Paul Walker, Frances O'Connor and Gerard Butler) excavating a 14th-century French fortress town known as Castlegard. Overseeing the dig is Professor Edward Johnston (Billy Connolly), a medieval expert who harbors growing suspicions concerning their mysterious benefactor, a techno-impresario named Robert Doninger (David Thewlis).

While Johnston flies to New Mexico to confront Doninger, his students unearth a chamber which had been sealed for 600 years. On the stone floor of the catacomb they find an anachronistic bifocal lens and, more amazing still, a parchment containing a plea for help written by Johnston -- which, defying explanation, is dated 1357. Unable to track down Johnston, they contact Doninger demanding answers.

They quickly learn that Doninger's think tank (a hush-hush corporate cabal called ITC) has inadvertently stumbled upon a time-travel process. In an effort to revolutionize the shipping business, ITC can now send humans back in time by "faxing" them through a quantum wormhole -- "faxing" being an apt means of transportation given the narrative's paper-thin characterizations. However, the particular wormhole in question seems to lead to only one destination, 14th-century France -- more specifically, Castlegard. Apparently, Johnston's curiosity got the better of his common sense.

Now that he's trapped six centuries in the past, it is up to his loyal students to rescue him; the only hitch is they have just six hours to do it. Donning medieval garb, they arrive as the English and French armies are gathering on the eve of one of the bloodiest battles of the Hundred Years' War -- which is about how long it feels like you have been sitting in the theater waiting for something to happen.

While sci-fi fans of the time-travel subgenre will have no problem suspending their disbelief (who cares if the characters' actions would alter history irreparably?), they may not be as forgiving when it comes to the film's overall cheesiness -- yes, one of the students even takes time out of his hectic rescue mission to ask a 14th-century French damsel if she is "seeing anyone."

Though full of clanging chain mail, the film's action centerpiece -- the siege of Castlegard -- feels rather small compared to the bar-raising grand-scale warfare depicted in such recent epics as "Braveheart," "Gladiator" and the "Lord of the Rings" trilogy.

Religion in the film is most noticeable by its absence. It is ironic that "Timeline" presents a 14th century -- one of the most devout eras in history -- with little reference to the role faith played in people's daily lives. In fact, the only scene containing any overtly religious elements involves two of the students desecrating a sacred fresco in a monastery in order to uncover a hidden passageway leading to the adjoining castle -- an act made more incredulous by the monks looking on and offering just minor objections.

While Crichton intended the story to show the hazards of medieval life, the only threats posed to viewers are choking on their popcorn while laughing at the harebrained dialogue or being up the rest of the night after sleeping through this snoozefest.

Walker, who takes the worst actor award -- an honor which, in all fairness, should be shared by the entire ensemble -- strolls through the film with a dumb the-drawbridge-is-down-but-nobody-is-home expression on his chiseled face. However, it would be unfair to put all the blame for this royal mess on Sir Walker the Wooden. Other knights errant in this fleur-de-listless fellowship include director Sir Donner of Schlock-berry and screenwriting squires Jeff Maguire and George Nolfi of North Hack-ford. By film's end, viewers may wish they had time machines of their own so they could travel back two hours and purchase tickets to a different movie.

Due to intense battle violence and some crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
